568.title: Their affairs by consultation
568.hook: the believers conduct their affairs by consultation (42:38)
568.howItsDone: Muslims treat shura, mutual consultation, as a value for families, communities and leadership; scholars have long debated how binding it is on leaders and what forms it should take.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ka-mithlihi, nothing like Him, who still hears and sees. Your line was beyond every picture, still listening.

Hudaybiya, near Mecca. The Prophet ﷺ has just signed a treaty that some of his companions find hard to accept. He tells them: get up, sacrifice your animals, and shave your heads. There will be no 'umra, no visit to the Kaaba, this year. Nobody moves. He says it three times. Still nobody. He goes into his tent, to his wife Umm Salama, and tells her what's happened. And she gives him advice that changes the afternoon. Bukhari records it. First, though, the verse that gives this surah its name.

Surah Ash-Shura, verse thirty-eight, part of a list describing the believers. Pickthall: "And those who answer the call of their Lord and establish worship, and whose affairs are a matter of counsel, and who spend of what We have bestowed on them." Look at the company consultation keeps: prayer on one side, giving on the other. Shura, consultation, sits right between them, as part of the description of a believer, not as a management tip. And the surah is counted among those revealed in Mecca, before there was any Muslim state, any government, any council. Consultation was a habit of believers before there was anything to govern. Back on day three hundred seventy-three, this path heard the Prophet told to consult his companions, even after a consultation went badly. Here, the believers do it with each other. Now, back to the tent at Hudaybiya. Umm Salama said: Messenger of Allah, do you want them to do it? Then go out, don't say a word to anyone, sacrifice your animal, and call your barber to shave your head. He did exactly that. When the companions saw him, they got up, sacrificed, and began shaving each other's heads, so eagerly, the report says, that they almost hurt each other. A prophet, receiving revelation, asked his wife what to do, and took her advice. Scholars point to this as a model: consultation isn't a formality, and good counsel can come from the person right beside you.

Think of one decision coming up, small or large: dinner, a trip, a change at work, a weekend, and who else it touches. Picture really asking them before you've decided, and wonder what they might see that you don't. Then rest, without carrying the decision alone.
Shura, consultation, the practice Ash-Shura names as part of being a believer, alongside prayer and giving. Today's word.
Your line: consult. In the verse, it sits between prayer and giving. Rest well; more tomorrow.

569.title: Daughters and sons
569.hook: He gives daughters to whom He wills, sons, or both, or none (42:49–50)
569.howItsDone: Muslims greet the birth of a child with thanks to Allah and often an 'aqiqah celebration for both girls and boys; the hadith on raising daughters is widely taught as an honor for parents of girls.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shura, consultation, set between prayer and giving. Your line was consult.

A man is told his wife has given birth to a girl. His face darkens. He hides from people, ashamed of the news, wondering whether to keep her or bury her in the dust. The Qur'an describes this scene from the Arabia it came down into, and it clearly wants the scene to end. Surah An-Nahl paints it; Surah At-Takwir says the buried girl will one day be asked for what sin she was killed. Against that background, listen to the order of the words in Surah Ash-Shura when it talks about children: who gets named first.

Verse forty-nine. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Pickthall: "He createth what He will." Then: He gives daughters to whomever He wills, and sons to whomever He wills. Daughters first. In a culture where a daughter's birth could darken a father's face, the Qur'an lists girls ahead of boys, as gifts. Some early scholars noticed this; one is reported to have said it's a blessing for a woman when her first child is a girl, because Allah began with daughters. Verse fifty continues: or He gives both, sons and daughters, and He makes whom He wills childless. He is Knowing, Able. Four possibilities: daughters, sons, both, or none, every one placed in Allah's hands. Teachers draw from this that none of them is a verdict on the parents. Not a reward for having sons. Not a punishment for having daughters, or no children at all. The Qur'an's stories and the Prophet's life bear it out. Ibrahim and Zakariyya were old when sons were given. 'A'isha, wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, had no children, and companions came to her with their questions. The Prophet himself had sons who died young, and it was through his daughter Fatima that his family continued. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives raising girls a special honor: whoever raises two daughters until they're grown, the Prophet said, will come on the Day of Resurrection with me like this, and he held two fingers together. The verse lists four gifts, and the hadith makes sure the first is never treated as the lesser.

Bring to mind the children around you, one by one: your own, if you have them, nieces and nephews, students, a friend's baby, the child you once were, and picture each face for a breath. If you pray, thank Allah for each one; if not, simply be grateful. And if there's an ache here, a child hoped for or lost, let it be part of the sitting too.
Hiba, gift, the sense behind Ash-Shura's yahab, Allah's giving of daughters, sons, both, or none, with daughters named first. Today's word.
Your line: each gift is his. Daughters, sons, both, or none, and none of it a verdict. That's day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: Silver roofs
570.hook: if not for people all becoming one in disbelief, the deniers would have had silver roofs, and it's all the enjoyment of this life (43:33–35)
570.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on zuhd, detachment from worldly things, often cites Az-Zukhruf 33–35 and the Prophet's simple room; many Muslims understand wealth as a trust to be used well, not a sign of God's favor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hiba, the gift of daughters, sons, both, or none, with daughters named first. Your line was each gift is his.

'Umar walks into a small room in Medina and finds the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lying on a rough mat of palm fiber, with nothing between it and his skin. When he sits up, the weave has left lines pressed into his side. A leather pillow stuffed with fiber. A little barley in the corner. 'Umar looks around and starts to cry. He's thinking of the kings of Persia and Rome in their palaces, and here is the Messenger of Allah on a mat. The Prophet asks him why he's crying. His answer, in Bukhari, is close to today's verses.

Surah Az-Zukhruf, verses thirty-three to thirty-five. The surah is pushing back on a claim it quotes a few verses earlier: if this message were true, wouldn't it have come to some great man of the two cities, someone rich? So the Qur'an answers with an image. If it weren't that all people would become one community of deniers, chasing it, Allah would have given those who deny the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and silver stairways to climb, and doors, and couches to lean on, and zukhruf, gold ornament. Then the verdict: all of that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the hereafter with your Lord is for the mindful. Commentators draw out the point: in this picture, silver roofs are so slight a thing they could be handed to people who reject Him, except that everyone would then chase the silver. Wealth isn't a sign of being favored, and it isn't the scale anyone is weighed on. Zukhruf, the surah's name, means gold, the ornament laid over a surface: beautiful, and on the outside. Back to 'Umar in the little room. The Prophet answered him: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? Not a rule against owning things; the companions included merchants and the wealthy. A rule about where the weight goes. And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says it more sharply: if this world were worth a mosquito's wing to Allah, He wouldn't give a denier a sip of water from it.

571.title: Friends that day
571.hook: friends that day will be enemies, except the mindful (43:67)
571.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to choose companions who help them toward good, and the hadith of the perfume seller and the blacksmith is often taught to young people about friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: silver roofs, the world's gold set beside the hereafter. Your line was ornaments pass.

Two shops on a market street. One sells perfume: walk in, and even if you buy nothing, you leave smelling good, or at least you've breathed something lovely for a few minutes. Next door, a blacksmith works the bellows: walk in there, and if a spark doesn't burn your clothes, you'll leave smelling of smoke. The Prophet ﷺ used exactly this picture, recorded in both Bukhari and Muslim, to describe friends. Surah Az-Zukhruf takes the same question, who your friends are, and follows it all the way to the Day.

Surah Az-Zukhruf, verse sixty-seven. Pickthall: "Friends on that day will be foes one to another, save those who kept their duty (to Allah)." The Arabic for friends is al-akhilla', the plural of khalil. Not an acquaintance: the closest kind of friend, the one whose love runs through you. Ibrahim is called Khalil Allah, the intimate friend of God. So the verse means the deepest friendships people have, and it says that on the Day many will turn into enmity. Why? Commentators explain: friendships built on doing wrong together, on vanity, on using each other, fall apart when everyone sees what they led to. Each friend blames the other. Another surah gives the voice of such a person: if only I hadn't taken so-and-so as a close friend. Then the exception: the muttaqin, the mindful, those who kept their duty. Friendships built on goodness don't break that day. The next verse turns straight to them: O My servants, no fear on you today, and you won't grieve. Words close to these came a few days ago in Fussilat, spoken by angels to those who stand firm. And the perfume seller comes back. A hadith in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi says a person follows the way of their close friend, so let each of you look at whom you befriend. When a man asked the Prophet about someone who loves a group but can't match their deeds, he answered, in Bukhari: a person will be with those they love. Choose your perfume sellers well.

Bring your closest friends to mind and, for each one, ask gently: when I leave time with them, do I smell of perfume or smoke, am I kinder, more honest, more patient? Don't judge anyone; just notice, and hold one friend who leaves you better. If you pray, ask that your friendships last beyond this life.
Khalil, the closest kind of friend, the bond Az-Zukhruf says breaks into enmity on the Day, except for the mindful. Today's word.
Your line: friends in goodness last. Perfume or smoke, it stays on you. Until tomorrow.

572.title: A blessed night
572.hook: We sent it down on a blessed night (44:3)
572.carry: a night better than a thousand months
572.howItsDone: Many Muslims spend the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan in extra prayer and Qur'an reading, seeking Laylat al-Qadr; some also keep the middle night of Sha'ban, and many pray a short night prayer before dawn year round.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalil, the closest friend, and the friendships that hold on the Day. Your line was friends in goodness last.

Plenty of books never say when they were written. The Qur'an speaks of its own coming down more than once, and here it names not a year or a season but a night. Surah Ad-Dukhan, the Smoke, the forty-fourth surah, begins with two Arabic letters, Ha and Mim, whose meaning, scholars say, Allah knows best. Then an oath by the book itself, and then, in the third verse, a time stamp. Not a date. A quality. The night it came down was blessed.

Pickthall's translation of the opening: "Ha. Mim. By the Scripture that maketh plain. Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night." The Arabic for blessed night is laylatin mubarakah. Mubarak comes from baraka, a word you may know from a greeting card: Eid Mubarak. Baraka is blessing that stays and grows, the way a little food somehow feeds a whole table. So which night is it? Ibn Kathir and most commentators say it's the night named in Surah Al-Qadr, the ninety-seventh surah: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, which hadith place in the last ten nights of Ramadan. Surah Al-Baqarah also says the Qur'an was revealed in the month of Ramadan, and putting those verses together, that reading became the common one. A minority of early voices connected this verse to the middle night of Sha'ban instead, and some Muslims still keep that night with prayer, but Ibn Kathir and others held to Ramadan. The next verse says that on this night every wise matter is made distinct, and commentators read that as the affairs of the coming year being set out, part of why people spend that night in prayer. And why a night at all? The Qur'an keeps coming back to the dark hours: rising for prayer while others sleep, the night as a covering. A night is when the noise stops. The sources don't explain why this book arrived after sunset rather than at noon, and it's honest to say so. But the people who keep the Night of Power answer with their feet: they stay awake, they pray, they read, waiting for a night better than a thousand months.

573.title: The smoke
573.hook: watch for the day the sky brings a visible smoke (44:10)
573.howItsDone: Muslims read Ad-Dukhan as part of the Qur'an's warnings; commentators teach both readings of the smoke, the famine in Mecca and a sign before the Last Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: baraka, and the blessed night the Qur'an came down. Your line was a night better than a thousand months.
screen: `A NIGHT BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.`

segments.voice: A man in a starving city looks up, and between him and the sky he sees something like smoke. Hold that picture; it comes from an early report. Surah Ad-Dukhan takes its name from one word in its tenth verse: dukhan, smoke. And the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not agree about what that smoke was. One of them thought it had already happened, in a hungry time in Mecca. Others thought it was still coming.

Here is the verse in plain words: watch for the day when the sky brings a smoke plain to see. The next verse says it will cover the people, a painful torment, and they cry out to their Lord to remove it. Then it will be lifted for a little while, and they will return to their ways. Two readings come down from the earliest generation. The first is from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Quraysh of Mecca resisted the Prophet so hard that he prayed against them, and a famine came, until people ate bones and carrion. A man would look up at the sky and see something like smoke between himself and it, from the hunger. Then the Meccans asked for relief, it came, and they went back to what they had been doing, just as the verses describe. For Ibn Mas'ud, the smoke was a past event. The second reading, linked to 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, says the smoke is one of the great signs before the Last Day. A hadith in Sahih Muslim lists ten signs before the Hour, and the smoke is among them. Some scholars hold both: a smoke that came, and a smoke still to come. In every reading, the shape stays the same. Something in the sky makes people afraid. They cry out. Relief comes. And then, very quickly, they forget they ever asked. The surah isn't only describing a catastrophe. It's describing how short human memory can be once the air clears.
screen: `WATCH FOR THE VISIBLE SMOKE.` · `IBN MAS'UD: A FAMINE IN MECCA.` · `OTHERS: A SIGN BEFORE THE HOUR.` · `THEY ASK, IT LIFTS, THEY FORGET.`

segments.voice: Breathe in through the nose and feel how cool the air is on the way in, how warm on the way out; you didn't earn it, and you didn't ask for it this morning. 574.title: Desire as a god
574.hook: have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god (45:23)
574.howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs and its hawa; many practice small refusals through voluntary fasts on Mondays and Thursdays, and classical spiritual writing treats taming desire as daily work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the smoke, a sign in the sky that people forget once it lifts. Your line was a sign in the sky.

It's eleven at night. You said you'd sleep early. One more episode. Then one more scroll. Then the fridge, for nothing in particular. Nobody forced any of it. Nobody would call it worship, either. It's just wanting, doing what wanting does when nobody stops it. But Surah Al-Jathiyah, the Kneeling, the forty-fifth surah, uses the language of worship for exactly that. It asks about a person whose wanting has quietly taken the top place in their life, the place the Qur'an keeps for God alone.

Pickthall's translation of verse twenty-three begins: "Hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god." The Arabic for desire is hawa. The dictionaries tie its root to falling, or being blown, the way something drops through the air with nothing under it. Hawa is wanting that pulls you along without asking where it's going. The verse doesn't say desire is evil. Muslim teaching makes room for appetite: food, marriage, rest, beauty, each in its place. The problem the verse names is rank. When the wanting decides and everything else obeys, the wanting has become a god, even if the person never bowed to an idol in their life. The rest of the verse is sobering: it speaks of hearing and heart sealed, and a covering on the sight. Many commentators read that as what slowly happens when every choice runs one way. Classical writers built a whole teaching on this. Al-Ghazali wrote at length about the struggle with the nafs, the self that wants, and used the picture of a mount and its rider: strong, useful, and safe only when the rider holds the reins. Surah An-Nazi'at praises the one who feared standing before his Lord and held the self back from hawa. So the word is not a word for sin. It's a word for direction. Is the mount carrying you, or are you being carried off? This week has moved through consultation, daughters and sons, silver roofs, friends that last, a blessed night and a smoke in the sky. It ends on a plain question: who, or what, sits on the throne inside you?
screen: `HAWA: DESIRE THAT PULLS YOU ALONG.` · `NOT EVIL, BUT OUT OF RANK.` · `THE SELF AS A MOUNT NEEDING A RIDER.` · `WHO SITS ON THE THRONE INSIDE?`

segments.voice: Let one small craving come up: a snack, your phone, a purchase, a reply you want to send too fast, and watch it the way you'd watch weather, noticing where it lives in the body. Then decide, quietly, that this one will wait until tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for help holding it.
Hawa. Desire that pulls you along, the wanting that 45:23 warns can take a god's place when nothing else is allowed to rank above it. Today's word.
Your line: not my desire's servant. The rider holds the reins. Day five hundred seventy-four, and the week is done.
